whyThisMatters: Crewing offers, payslips, and reference-check forms are routine work for HR — which is exactly why attackers copy them so closely. A slightly different domain or an attachment that needs "Enable Content" can hide inside a message that otherwise looks like any other day's work. Today you will build the habit of checking the sender's exact domain and the file type before you open or act on anything that touches pay or a candidate's details.
rememberThis: A professional-looking offer letter, payslip, or reference form is not proof by itself. STOP before opening an attachment or updating any bank or candidate detail — VERIFY the sender's exact domain and, for anything financial, through the portal you already use — then REPORT anything that doesn't match.

discussionPrompts: Ask which detail people noticed first on the spear-phishing card — the sender's exact domain, or did the personal name and real detail make them skip that check?
For the fake login portal, ask how many people actually check the address bar before typing a password on a page that already looks exactly right.
For the QR-code notice, ask who has ever scanned a printed code without checking where it led afterward — what would make that habit stick?
Ask why a 'confidential, don't discuss' instruction from a senior title is the actual warning sign, not a reason to comply faster.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often miss the spear-phishing and fake-login-portal cards, because a real name/detail or an exact visual copy both feel like proof on their own. The habit to build is the same one used everywhere else: check the exact sending domain or address bar letter by letter — personalisation, visual accuracy, and seniority are all things attackers can fake, none of them are the actual proof.

items.title: Real vs Fake Crewing Offer Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake Crewing email comes from hr@synergymarinegr0up.com — the letter "o" has been replaced with a zero, which looks almost identical in most fonts. The real address is hr@synergymarinegroup.com. The subject line, logo, and body look identical — only that single swapped character in the sender address is different.
items.whyItsSuspicious: This is a homoglyph attack — a single swapped character that looks nearly identical to the real letter, easy to miss when reading fast. Crewing teams email people they have never met, so there's no familiar sender to compare against from memory. The safest habit is to compare the address character by character against a copy you already trust, not just glance at it. If you are not sure, call the known HR crewing number you already have; do not reply to the address in the email.

items.title: Real vs Fake Payslip & Roster Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake HR Payroll email has unexpected attachments. One is Payslip_March.pdf.exe — the name ends with .exe, which means it is actually an app, not a PDF. The other is a generic Documents.zip with a password "1234" given in the email. It asks you to "Enable Content" or enter the password. The real payslip email has expected files with clear names: Payslip_Feb2025_RajKumar.pdf and Rotation_Roster_MV-Horizon_Feb-Apr.xlsx, with matching icons and sensible file sizes.
items.whyItsSuspicious: HR Payroll often sends payslips and rotation rosters, so fake attachments blend in. Ask yourself: did you expect this file? Does the name and type match what you were waiting for? A payslip should be a PDF; a roster should be a spreadsheet. You should never need to click "Enable Content" or enter a password to open them. Watch for double endings like .pdf.exe, generic ZIP files, or vague subjects like "Updated Payslip — Please Review Immediately." If unsure, call HR Payroll on a known number before you open anything.

items.title: Real vs Fake Payroll Password Reset Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from payroll-systems@synergymarinegroup.co — the address is missing the final "m" in ".com", which is very easy to miss, especially on a phone screen. It asks you to sign in through a link instead of the portal you already use, with an invented migration deadline tied to a service interruption.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A dropped letter at the very end of a domain is one of the easiest changes to miss — most people stop reading a familiar-looking address after the first few words. The link itself looks harmless ("sign in to continue"), which is exactly the point — the real danger is the page it actually leads to, not the button text. A genuine system migration is announced through the portal itself and known internal channels; sign in by typing the address you already know, never by clicking a link in an email.

items.title: Real vs Fake Reference Check Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from references@crewsolutlons-asia.com — the "i" in "solutions" has been replaced with a lowercase "l", which reads almost identically at normal size. Its attachment is a macro-enabled document instead of a plain form, and it asks for it back today because the candidate starts Monday.
items.whyItsSuspicious: An "i" and a lowercase "l" look nearly identical in many fonts, which is exactly why this substitution is used — recognising an agent's name is not the same as checking the domain letter by letter. Recruitment routinely receives forms and CVs from agents, so a fake one blends in easily. A reference form should never need "Enable Content" to open, regardless of how close the domain looks to the real one.

items.title: Real vs Fake Bank-Details Confirmation Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from hr-payroll@synergymarinegroup.net — everything before the domain is identical to the real address, only the final ".net" instead of ".com" is different. Its subject line stays fairly generic ("Payroll Details Confirmation Needed"), but the body asks you to reply with your bank account number and IFSC/SWIFT code directly, with an invented threat of "payment failure".
items.whyItsSuspicious: A changed top-level domain (.net instead of .com) is one of the subtlest possible tells, since the rest of the address matches exactly — checking the full address, including the ending, matters every time, not just the part that looks familiar. Real HR Payroll processes only ever point you to update your own bank details yourself inside the portal — they never ask you to email your account number and IFSC/SWIFT code back to them, however routine the subject line sounds.

items.title: Real vs Fake Personalized Follow-Up Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from r.fernandes@synergymaarinegroup.com — the letter "a" is doubled in "marine", which is easy to read past at normal speed. It uses the recipient's real first name and a genuine recent event (a transfer request) to feel personal, then asks you to click through to "review and confirm a couple of details" without saying exactly what for.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A doubled letter is a small enough change that most people's eyes correct for it automatically while reading — which is exactly why it works. Notice the ask itself is deliberately vague ("a couple of details") — a real attacker rarely announces exactly what they're after up front, since a vague, low-effort-sounding click is easier to get than an alarming one. Personalising an email with your real name and a real recent event is called spear-phishing; a message being personal is not proof it's genuine, and neither is a button that sounds harmless — the sender's exact domain, read slowly, is still the only real check.

items.title: Real vs Fake HR Self-Service Login Portal
items.whatIsWrong: The fake portal's address is portal.synergymarinegroup-hr.com/hr — it starts with the exact real domain you recognise, but "-hr" has been appended right before the real top-level domain, making the actual registered domain something else entirely. The login page itself is copied exactly, so only the address bar, read in full, gives it away.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Attackers know you recognise the start of a familiar address, so they add extra text right before the real ending to exploit that — the part of a domain that actually matters is immediately before ".com", not whatever comes first. Always read the full address, especially right around the final domain ending, before typing your password, and open the portal from a bookmark you saved yourself rather than a link.

items.title: Real vs Fake Printed Benefits Enrolment Notice
items.whatIsWrong: The fake notice's QR code has been swapped — a sticker placed over the original — and it leads to portal.synergymarinegroup.com.benefits-enrol.net. It looks like it starts with the real portal address, but everything after "synergymarinegroup.com" here is actually part of a different domain, benefits-enrol.net, not a page on your own portal. It also invents a same-day deadline ("closes TODAY") the real notice never had.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Putting a familiar domain at the start of a web address is a classic trick — a browser or QR scanner only reads the domain immediately before the final "/", which here is benefits-enrol.net, not synergymarinegroup.com. A QR code hides its destination until you scan it, so this trick is even easier to miss on a phone screen. Always check the full address your phone shows before you continue past the scan, and type the known portal address directly when in doubt.

items.title: Real vs Fake HR Director Payroll Instruction
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from s.almeida@synergymarinegroup.cm — the domain is missing the final "o" in ".com", a single-character drop that's very easy to miss when a senior name and urgent tone hold your attention instead. It has no reference number tying it to the normal payroll batch process, and it explicitly instructs you to process it personally, outside the usual system, and keep it confidential.
items.whyItsSuspicious: A single missing letter at the very end of a domain is designed to be overlooked, especially when a senior title and confidentiality are already pulling your focus elsewhere. This is a whaling attack — using seniority and secrecy as pressure to bypass a normal process, the same pattern as any Business Email Compromise attempt just aimed at payroll instead of Accounts. A genuine payroll change always references the existing batch/approval process, checked with the full domain read to its very last character.
